narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest reasons the model leaned toward failure. Being in the bottom decile for both Year 1 and Year 3 grades—compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students—strongly pushed the prediction toward not passing the bar. These academic performance signals carried more weight than anything else in your profile.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.00, which is modestly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, worked in the opposite direction. It actually gave the model a small reason to expect you might pass, but this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the much stronger negative signals from your class rankings.

Your family income, LSAT score of 33, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or consider a post-baccalaureate program that can demonstrate higher performance. Raising your LSAT score would also help offset the earlier ranking concerns. Consider reapplying once you have clearer evidence that you can excel in demanding coursework.
